chapters.title: Chapter 4 · The Queen's Garden
chapters.artPrompt: three flat playing-card gardeners with paint pots colouring white roses red on a rose tree, a little girl in a blue dress watching in a palace garden of fountains and flower beds, bright morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text:
Alice had seen enough of the mad tea-party. 'At any rate, I'll never go there again,' she said. 'It's the stupidest tea-party I ever was at in all my life!' So she got up and walked off. The Hatter and the March Hare were trying to push the Dormouse into the teapot. Alice did not stop to watch.

In the wood she came to a tree with a little door in it. She opened the door and stepped through. Then she gave a jump of joy. She was back in the long hall, beside the little glass table! The tiny golden key still lay upon it.

This time Alice knew just what to do. She still had a piece of mushroom in her pocket. A Caterpillar had once told her that it could make her grow small or tall. She nibbled a little, and soon she was only a foot high. Then she took the key, unlocked the garden door, and crept through. At last she stood in the most beautiful garden she had ever seen. There were cool fountains and beds of the loveliest flowers.
Three playing-card gardeners paint the white roses red in the Queen's garden.

Close by stood a rose-tree covered with white roses. Three gardeners were busy painting the flowers red! They were flat and oblong, like playing cards, with arms and legs at the corners. Their names were Two, Five and Seven.

'Would you tell me,' said Alice, 'why you are painting those roses?' Five and Seven said nothing, but Two spoke. 'You see, Miss, this tree ought to have been a red rose-tree. We planted a white one by mistake. If the Queen finds out, we shall all have our heads cut off!'
New word: procession — a long line of people walking one after another in a grand parade.

Just then a cry ran through the garden: 'The Queen! The Queen!' First came ten soldiers carrying clubs. Then came ten courtiers covered with diamonds, and the ten royal children, all hearts. Close to them came the White Rabbit, talking in a nervous whisper. Last of all walked the King and Queen of Hearts.

The Queen was shouting, 'Off with his head!' at everyone she met. Alice felt a little afraid. Then she remembered that they were only a pack of cards. 'I needn't be afraid of them!' she said to herself.
Talk together: Why did the gardeners paint the roses red instead of telling the truth? Would you tell the Queen the truth?

'What's your name, child?' the Queen asked. 'My name is Alice, so please your Majesty,' said Alice politely. Then the Queen pointed at the three gardeners, who lay flat on their faces. 'And who are these?' Alice could not tell. The Queen turned crimson with fury. 'Off with their heads!' she screamed. But Alice quickly hid the gardeners in a large flower-pot. 'Are their heads off?' the Queen shouted. 'Their heads are gone, if it please your Majesty!' the soldiers called back. 'That's right!' said the Queen. 'Can you play croquet?' she asked Alice. 'Yes!' said Alice loudly. 'Come on, then!' And Alice walked on, wondering what would happen next.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 · Croquet with Flamingos
chapters.artPrompt: a little girl in a blue dress swinging a pink flamingo like a croquet mallet towards a curled-up hedgehog ball, playing-card soldiers bent down as arches on a sunny palace lawn, storybook illustration

blocks.text:
The croquet-ground was full of players, all shouting at once. Alice had never heard such a noisy game. The balls were live hedgehogs. The mallets were live flamingoes. The soldiers lay on their faces and hands to make the arches.

Alice soon found that this game was very hard indeed. Her flamingoe kept twisting its head round to look at her. Whenever she was ready to strike, the hedgehog would walk slowly away. And there were no rules at all.

'Off with his head! Off with her head!' cried the Queen, about once a minute. Alice began to feel very uneasy. 'They are dreadfully fond of beheading people here,' she thought. 'The great wonder is that there's anyone left alive!'
Alice plays croquet with a flamingo for a mallet and a hedgehog for a ball.

The other players had stopped playing, for everyone was quarrelling. Just then Alice saw something in the air above her. It was the grin of the Cheshire Cat, and slowly the eyes and the rest of it appeared.

'How are you getting on?' said the Cat. Alice waited till its ears came, then told it all her troubles. 'I don't think they play at all fairly,' she said. 'How do you like the Queen?' the Cat asked in a low voice. 'Not at all,' said Alice. 'She's so extremely—' Then she saw the Queen close behind her, and quickly finished: '—likely to win!'
New word: croquet — an outdoor game where players hit balls through little arches with long mallets. Wonderland croquet is much stranger!

The King soon noticed the floating head. 'Who is this?' he asked. 'It's a friend of mine — a Cheshire Cat,' said Alice. 'Allow me to introduce it.' 'I don't like it at all,' said the King. But the Cat only grinned more and more. 'A cat may look at a king,' said Alice. 'You have heard that saying, I think?'

The King sent for the executioner at once. 'Cut off its head!' cried the Queen. But how could he? The executioner said you cannot cut off a head unless there is a body to cut it from. The King said anything that has a head can be beheaded. The Queen said if nothing was done quickly, everybody would be executed all round! While they argued, the Cat's head slowly faded away.
Talk together: The Cheshire Cat can vanish piece by piece. Which part of the Cat would you like to see first?

'It's gone!' cried the King, hunting everywhere for the Cat. Alice said quietly that the Cat belonged to the Duchess. 'The Duchess is in prison,' snapped the Queen, 'because she boxed my ears.' Then she called across the ground, 'Fetch the Duchess here!' The game went on, but Alice was growing tired of it. Soon the Duchess came hurrying towards her, smiling from ear to ear.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · The Duchess and Her Morals
chapters.artPrompt: a large friendly Duchess in a shawl walking arm in arm with a little girl in a blue dress on a palace lawn, the Duchess holding up one finger as she gives advice, warm afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text:
'You can't think how glad I am to see you again, you dear old thing!' cried the Duchess. She tucked her arm into Alice's, and off they walked together. Alice was glad to find the Duchess in such a pleasant temper. Perhaps it was only the pepper that made her so cross, thought Alice.

'You're thinking about something, my dear,' said the Duchess, 'and that makes you forget to talk.' 'I was only thinking about the game,' said Alice, feeling a little shy. 'Tut, tut, child!' said the Duchess. 'Everything's got a moral, if only you can find it.' And she kept squeezing Alice's arm as they went.
The Duchess walks arm in arm with Alice, finding a moral in everything.

'The game is going on rather better now,' Alice said politely. ''Tis, 'tis,' said the Duchess. 'And the moral of that is — 'Oh, 'tis love, 'tis love, that makes the world go round!''

'Flamingoes and mustard both bite,' the Duchess went on. 'And the moral of that is — 'Birds of a feather flock together.'' 'But mustard isn't a bird,' said Alice. 'Right, as usual,' said the Duchess. 'What a clear way you have of putting things!'
New word: moral — a little lesson about life, often found at the end of a story. The Duchess finds one in everything!

Just then the Queen came stamping up to them. 'Now I give you fair warning!' she shouted. 'Either you or your head must be off! Off with her head!' In a moment the Duchess had vanished. Alice was not one bit sorry.

The Queen led Alice back to the croquet-ground. On the way, the King quietly pardoned all the prisoners. That was a good thing! Then the Queen asked, 'Have you seen the Mock Turtle yet?' 'No,' said Alice. 'I don't even know what a Mock Turtle is.' 'It's the thing Mock Turtle Soup is made from,' said the Queen. 'Come on. He shall tell you his history.'
Talk together: The Duchess says everything has a moral. Can you find a little lesson in something that happened to you today?

The Queen found the Gryphon lying fast asleep in the sun. 'Up, lazy thing!' she cried. 'Take this young lady to see the Mock Turtle. I must go back and order some executions.' Then she walked away. 'What fun!' said the Gryphon, half to itself, half to Alice. 'What is the fun?' Alice asked. 'Why, she never executes nobody, you know,' it whispered. 'Come on!' And off they went. 'Everybody says 'come on' here,' thought Alice, as she followed.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · The Mock Turtle's Story
chapters.artPrompt: a weeping mock turtle with a calf's head and a shell sitting on a rock by the sea, a little girl in a blue dress and a gryphon listening quietly, golden evening light on the waves, storybook illustration

blocks.text:
The Gryphon was a very strange creature, half eagle and half lion. It led Alice to a rock by the sea. There sat the Mock Turtle, sighing and sighing, with tears running down his cheeks.

'This here young lady wants to know your history,' said the Gryphon. 'I'll tell it her,' said the Mock Turtle in a deep, sad voice. 'Sit down, both of you, and don't speak a word till I've finished.'

The Mock Turtle began, slowly and sadly. 'Once,' he sighed, 'I was a real Turtle.' Then he hid his face in his paws. Alice wanted to say something kind, but no words would come.
The sad Mock Turtle tells his story to Alice and the Gryphon.

'When we were little,' the Mock Turtle went on, 'we went to school in the sea. The master was an old Turtle. We used to call him Tortoise.' 'Why did you call him Tortoise, if he wasn't one?' Alice asked. 'We called him Tortoise because he taught us,' said the Mock Turtle crossly. 'Really, you are very dull!'

'What lessons did you have?' Alice asked quickly. 'Reeling and Writhing, of course,' said the Mock Turtle. 'That is, reading and writing, the sea way. Then we had the four branches of Arithmetic — Ambition, Distraction, Uglification and Derision.' 'I never heard of Uglification,' said Alice.

'How many hours a day did you have lessons?' Alice asked. 'Ten hours the first day,' said the Mock Turtle, 'nine the next, and so on.' 'What a curious plan!' cried Alice. 'That's why they're called lessons,' the Gryphon put in. 'Because they lessen from day to day.'
Talk together: Say 'he taught us' and 'Tortoise' out loud. Do they sound almost the same? That is the joke!

'I only took the regular course,' the Mock Turtle went on with a sigh. 'I couldn't afford the extras.' 'What are the extras?' Alice asked. 'French and music,' said the Mock Turtle. 'And washing too?' Alice asked. 'Certainly not,' said the Mock Turtle. 'Washing was extra. We never had any of that in the sea!'
New word: extra — something you may have at school, but only if you pay more. Even fish school has extras!

'Then the eleventh day must have been a holiday!' said Alice. 'Of course it was,' said the Mock Turtle. 'And what about the twelfth?' Alice began. But the Gryphon cut her short. 'That's enough about lessons,' it said in a decided tone. 'Tell her something about the games now.'

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Lobster Quadrille
chapters.artPrompt: a mock turtle with a calf's head and a gryphon dancing hand in hand on a sandy shore, tossing a lobster towards the waves while a little girl in a blue dress watches, bright seaside light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: 'You can have no idea what a delightful thing a Lobster Quadrille is!' cried the Mock Turtle. 'No, indeed,' said Alice. 'What sort of a dance is it?' 'Why,' said the Gryphon, 'you first form into a line along the sea-shore.' 'Two lines!' cried the Mock Turtle. 'Seals, turtles, salmon and so on. Then you clear all the jelly-fish away—' 'That generally takes some time,' said the Gryphon. '—then you advance twice, each with a lobster as a partner!' 'Of course,' the Mock Turtle went on. 'You throw the lobsters out to sea! You swim after them! You turn a somersault in the sea! Then you change lobsters and come back on shore. That's the first figure.'
The Mock Turtle and the Gryphon dance the Lobster Quadrille for Alice.
New word: quadrille — an old-fashioned dance for groups of dancers. Wonderland dancers use lobsters as partners!

'Would you like to see it?' the Mock Turtle asked. 'Very much indeed,' said Alice. The two creatures got up and danced. They hopped round and round Alice, sometimes treading on her toes. The Mock Turtle sang slowly and sadly: 'Will you walk a little faster?' said a whiting to a snail. 'There's a porpoise close behind us, and he's treading on my tail.'

'It is certainly a very pretty dance,' said Alice politely, when it was over. Then she asked why a fish would want a porpoise with him. 'No wise fish goes anywhere without a porpoise,' said the Mock Turtle. 'Don't you mean purpose?' said Alice. The Mock Turtle only sobbed.
Talk together: No wise fish travels without a 'porpoise'. Can you hear another word hiding inside porpoise?

After that, the Mock Turtle sang a song about a lobster. 'You have baked me too brown, I must sugar my hair!' he sang. Then came his favourite song of all. It was about beautiful soup, so rich and green, waiting in a hot tureen. 'Beautiful Soup! Beau-ootiful Soo-oop!' he sang, waving his paws. The Gryphon joined in loudly. 'Chorus again!' it cried, when the song was done.

Just as the Mock Turtle began the song once more, a cry came from far away: 'The trial is beginning!' 'Come on!' cried the Gryphon. It caught Alice's hand and hurried her away. 'What trial is it?' Alice panted as they ran. But the Gryphon only cried, 'Come on!' Alice ran as fast as she could. Behind her, the Mock Turtle's sad song died slowly away.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · Who Stole the Tarts?
chapters.artPrompt: the King and Queen of Hearts on a grand throne in a garden court, playing-card guards, a chained knave and a dish of golden tarts on a table, twelve small animals in a jury box, bright afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text:
Alice and the Gryphon reached the court. The King and Queen of Hearts sat on the throne, and a great crowd stood round them. There were little birds, little beasts, and the whole pack of cards. In the middle of the court stood a table. On it lay a large dish of tarts.

In chains, before them, sat the Knave of Hearts. The King himself was the judge. He wore his crown over his great wig, and he did not look at all comfortable. Twelve little creatures sat in the jury-box, all busy writing on their slates. The White Rabbit stood near the King, with a trumpet and a scroll of parchment.
The court: the King and Queen on their thrones, and the tarts on the table.

'What are they doing?' Alice whispered to the Gryphon. 'They are putting down their names,' said the Gryphon. 'They are afraid of forgetting them before the end of the trial.' One juror, Bill the Lizard, could not write. His pencil only made a squeaking noise. So the Gryphon took the pencil and wrote his name for him. Alice could see the words on their slates. Every single one said 'Stupid things!'
New word: jury — a group of people who listen at a trial and decide whether someone is guilty.

The Herald read out the accusation. 'The Queen of Hearts, she made some tarts, all on a summer day. The Knave of Hearts, he stole those tarts, and took them quite away!'

'Consider your verdict,' said the King. 'Not yet, not yet!' said the White Rabbit hastily. 'There's a great deal to come before that!' 'Call the first witness,' said the King.
Talk together: The Knave is accused of stealing tarts. Do you think he did it? What would count as good proof?

The White Rabbit blew three loud blasts upon his trumpet. 'Witness! Hatter!' he called. In came the Hatter, with a teacup in one hand and a piece of bread-and-butter in the other. 'I beg pardon, your Majesty,' he began, 'for bringing these in. I hadn't quite finished my tea when I was sent for.' 'You ought to have finished,' said the King. 'When did you begin?' The Hatter looked at the March Hare, who had followed him into court arm in arm with the Dormouse. 'Fourteenth of March, I think it was,' he said. 'Fifteenth,' said the March Hare. 'Sixteenth,' added the Dormouse.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · The Hatter's Evidence
chapters.artPrompt: a nervous top-hatted hatter standing in a witness box holding a teacup and bread-and-butter, a cross King with a crown over his wig pointing at him, playing-card guards and animal courtiers nearby, storybook illustration

blocks.text: 'Give your evidence,' said the King. 'And don't be nervous, or I'll have you executed on the spot.' The poor Hatter trembled so much that he shook off both his shoes. 'I'm a poor man, your Majesty,' he began. 'And you're a very poor speaker,' said the King. Here one of the guinea-pigs cheered. Officers at once put him into a large canvas bag. They tied up the mouth of it and carried him off. Alice was glad to see some of the jury write that down.
The nervous Hatter gives his evidence, still holding his teacup.
New word: witness — a person who tells the court what they know about the case.

'After that,' the Hatter went on, 'I cut some more bread-and-butter.' 'But what did the Dormouse say?' asked the King. The Queen put on her spectacles and stared hard at the Hatter. The poor Hatter turned pale and dropped both his teacup and his bread-and-butter. 'You may go,' said the King. The Hatter left the court in great haste, without even putting on his shoes. The March Hare and the Dormouse followed him. 'And just take his head off outside,' the Queen called to one of the officers.

The next witness was the Duchess's cook. She carried her pepper-box, and everyone near her began to sneeze. 'Give your evidence,' said the King. 'Shan't,' said the cook. Then the sleepy Dormouse began talking in his sleep. 'Turn that Dormouse out! Pinch him! Off with his whiskers!' cried the Queen. For a minute or two the whole court was in confusion. When they had all settled down again, the cook had disappeared.
Talk together: The King tells the Hatter not to be nervous. Does that help? What would help you feel brave?

Just then Alice felt a very curious feeling. She was beginning to grow again! At first she thought she ought to rise and leave the court. But on second thoughts she decided to stay. 'You have no right to grow here,' said Bill the Lizard beside her. 'Don't talk nonsense,' said Alice. 'You know you are growing too.' 'Yes, but I grow at a reasonable pace,' said the Lizard. 'Not in that ridiculous fashion.' Then the White Rabbit blew his trumpet once more. 'Witness!' he called. 'Alice!'

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · Alice's Evidence
chapters.artPrompt: a tall brave girl in a blue dress standing before the King and Queen of Hearts on their throne, a storm of flying playing cards swirling towards her, an animal courtroom scattering in all directions, dramatic light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: 'Here!' cried Alice. She jumped up in such a hurry that she tipped over the jury-box. All the little jurymen tumbled head over heels on to the floor. 'The trial cannot proceed,' said the King very gravely, 'until all the jurymen are back in their proper places.' Alice picked them all up and put them back as quickly as she could. Poor Bill the Lizard was left hanging head-down over the edge, so she lifted him out and set him right.
Alice, grown tall, stands up to the angry court of cards.
New word: verdict — the jury's answer at the end of a trial: did the person do it, or not?

'What do you know about this business?' the King asked. 'Nothing,' said Alice. 'Nothing whatever?' 'Nothing whatever,' said Alice. 'That's very important,' said the King, and the jurymen wrote it down. They wrote 'unimportant' where 'important' should have been.

Then the King read out from his rule-book: 'Rule Forty-two. All persons more than a mile high must leave the court.' Everybody stared at Alice. 'I'm not a mile high,' said Alice. 'You are,' said the King. 'Nearly two miles high,' added the Queen. 'Well, I shan't go,' said Alice. 'That's not a regular rule. You invented it just now.' 'It's the oldest rule in the book,' said the King. 'Then it ought to be Number One,' said Alice. The King turned quite pale and shut his notebook in a hurry.

'There's more evidence yet, please your Majesty,' said the White Rabbit, jumping up in a great hurry. He held out a paper. 'What is it?' asked the Queen. The Rabbit unfolded it. 'It isn't a letter, it's a set of verses,' he said. The verses were not in the Knave's handwriting, but nobody minded that. The King said they were the most important evidence of all. He read them out to the court. They were the queerest verses Alice had ever heard. 'If anyone can explain them,' said Alice, 'I'll give him sixpence. I don't believe there's an atom of meaning in them.' 'If there's no meaning in it,' said the King, 'that saves a world of trouble. We needn't try to find any.'
Talk together: Alice finally says what she thinks, even to a Queen. Was that brave? When is it good to speak up?

'Consider your verdict,' the King said to the jury. 'No, no!' said the Queen. 'Sentence first — verdict afterwards!' 'Stuff and nonsense!' said Alice loudly. 'The idea of having the sentence first!' 'Hold your tongue!' said the Queen, turning purple. 'I won't!' said Alice. 'Off with her head!' the Queen shouted at the top of her voice. Alice had grown to her full size by this time. She was not a bit afraid. 'Who cares for you?' she said. 'You're nothing but a pack of cards!' At this the whole pack rose up into the air. They came flying down upon her, little sharp points and all.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · Alice Wakes Up
chapters.artPrompt: a little girl waking on a sunny riverbank with her head in her older sister's lap, golden leaves drifting down, the river sparkling behind them, warm late afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text:
Alice gave a little scream, half of fright and half of anger. She tried to beat the cards away. Then her hands closed on nothing at all. She was lying on the river bank, with her head in her sister's lap. A few dead leaves had fluttered down from the trees on to her face. Her sister was gently brushing them away. The warm sun was still shining on the river.

'Oh, I've had such a curious dream!' said Alice. She told her sister all about it. There was the White Rabbit, the mad tea-party, the Queen of Hearts, and the Mock Turtle. It had all seemed very real as she spoke. But her sister only smiled. 'It was a curious dream, dear, certainly,' she said. 'But now run in to your tea. It's getting late.' So Alice got up and ran off. While she ran, she thought what a wonderful dream it had been.
Alice wakes with her head in her sister's lap, safe by the river.
Talk together: What was your favourite part of Alice's dream? Who would you like to meet in Wonderland?

Her sister stayed on the bank with her chin in her hand. She watched the setting sun, and half fell asleep herself. She seemed to see Wonderland too. The rattling tea-cups turned into the tinkling of sheep bells. The Queen's shrill cries became the voice of the shepherd boy. The Mock Turtle's sad sobs sounded like the lowing of cattle far away. Every sound of the evening seemed full of Wonderland. Then she thought about her little sister. One day Alice would be a grown woman. She would keep her kind, simple heart, even then.
New word: curious — strange and interesting. Alice calls her dream 'curious' because so many odd things happened in it.

She pictured Alice grown up, with children of her own gathered round her. Alice would tell them wonderful tales, and make their eyes bright and eager. Perhaps she would even tell them the dream of Wonderland, from long, long ago. She would feel all their small sorrows, and enjoy all their simple joys. Then the sister thought of those happy summer days, and the little girl who had dreamed them. The end.
